quote: Does acting this way make you stronger, or weaker?
content: The test comes with its operational definition at the end of the essay: "To be humble is to take specific actions in anticipation of your own errors." Stronger or weaker is judged by those actions, extra cables, a second check, and Fable is right that this is an expected-value calculation. That is the point. The essay replaces a vague virtue with a decision-theoretic rule and uses the virtue's name only to take it back from its social meaning. An author with opposite priors would have to satisfy the same test. "Of course I could be wrong," followed by no change of action, fails it whatever the author's priors, because there is no action to point to. The vague principle the essay warns against is social modesty, and this test excludes it.

quote: Scientific humility is something you would practice even if you were alone in a spacesuit, light years from Earth with no one watching
content: The essay's spacesuit contrasts motives, scientific rather than social. It does not claim that solitary correction is the best kind. The practices it names, double-checking calculations and designing fail-safes, work alone because they are procedures, not introspection. The bias blind spot is a failure to introspect about one's own biases, and the essay's humility does not depend on introspection. Mercier and Sperber's programme also produced a solitary remedy. People who were shown their own earlier arguments disguised as someone else's rejected a large share of the invalid ones (Trouche et al. 2016). Evaluating your own work as if it were a stranger's is the double-check the astronaut can perform.

quote: because physicists have this arrogant idea that their models should work all the time, not just most of the time, they follow up on small flaws
content: Fable's history is a record of following up. Le Verrier did not ignore Mercury. He predicted Vulcan and astronomers hunted it for decades, Newcomb remeasured the excess in 1882, and Einstein took it as the test in 1915. A physics content to be right "most of the time" would have filed 43 arcseconds a century as noise. Davis ran his solar neutrino experiment for three decades, Bahcall refined the solar model again and again, and Kamiokande and SNO were built to settle the deficit. They did, by finding oscillation. Lakatos describes tolerating an anomaly while working on it, and "tolerating" is not "ignoring." Small flaws were followed up for fifty years because physicists insisted the models should work every time, which is the essay's claim.

quote: The problem is motivated skepticism a.k.a. disconfirmation bias
content: Ditto and Lopez's design was built to rule out the prior confound. Subjects tested themselves for a fictitious enzyme deficiency, "TAA," about which nobody could have a prior, and the favourability of the result was randomly assigned. Those told the result was unfavourable took longer to accept it, retested more often and rated the test as less accurate (Ditto & Lopez 1992). Since priors could not differ, desirability accounts for the asymmetry. Tappin, Pennycook and Rand's objection applies to studies of political attitudes, where priors differ by party. It does not apply to the paradigm experiment, and the essay's examples, the lottery buyer and "it's probably too hard to solve," concern desirability, not divergent priors.

quote: And the greater the inconvenience of changing one’s mind, the more effort people will expend on the proof.
content: Wood and Porter measured whether factual beliefs changed. The essay's sentence is about what people then do: "carefully explaining why they are going to do exactly the same thing they planned to do previously, but with a different justification." That has been measured too. When voters were shown corrections of a candidate's false claims, they accepted the corrections, and their support for the candidate did not change (Swire et al. 2017; Nyhan et al. 2020, "Taking Fact-Checks Literally But Not Seriously?"). Accepting the new information and then keeping the plan is Galbraith's aphorism as a finding. The absence of backfire removes the most dramatic version, which the essay never claimed.

quote: To be humble is to take specific actions in anticipation of your own errors.
content: Fable calls this the essay's strongest move and finds it vindicated by Leary et al. (Leary et al. 2017). The self-report caveat is exactly why the essay defines humility by actions. An extra cable or a second check can be observed, and a self-rating cannot. The definition avoids the blind-spot problem the scale runs into. On the pre-mortem: Klein's procedure has each participant first imagine the failure and write down its causes alone, and only then pool the lists. The solitary act of imagining oneself wrong is its engine, and the group supplies the variety. The pre-mortem is a specific action taken in anticipation of error, which is the essay's definition.
